modules.name: Reaction Mechanisms and Types of Cleavage

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Reaction Mechanisms:

  • The step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions involved in a chemical change.
Types of Cleavage:

  • Homolytic Cleavage: Equal splitting of bonds, forming free radicals ( carbon free radicals).
  • Heterolytic Cleavage: Unequal splitting of bonds, producing ions ( carbo-cation & carbanion)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electrophiles:

  • Electron-deficient species seeking electrons.
  • Can accept electron pairs.
  • Positively charged or neutral with a vacant orbital & polar pi bond containing.
  • Examples: $$, $SO_3$,$BF_3$, $NO_2^+$,  RCHO, RCOR etc.
Nucleophiles:

  • Electron-rich species donate electron pairs.
  • Negatively charged or neutral with lone pairs & non-polar pi bonds.
  • Examples: $OH^-$, $NH_3$, $Cl^-$, Alkene, Alkyne. etc.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not recognizing that neutral molecules can be electrophiles if they have vacant orbitals (e.g., $BF_3$).
$NH_4^+$ is not an electrophile even it carries positive charge because its octet is complete.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: Identify the electrophile and nucleophile in the reaction: $CH_3Cl + OH^- \rightarrow CH_3OH + Cl^-$.
blocks.prompt: Identify the electrophile and nucleophile in the reaction: $CH_3Cl + OH^- \rightarrow CH_3OH + Cl^-$.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Carbocations:

  • Positively charged carbon species.
  • Often intermediates in reactions.
  • Electron deficient  and trigonal planar structure ($sp^2$) hybridization with one vacant p-orbital and that p orbital is perpendicular to the trigonal plane).
Carbanions:

  • Negatively charged carbon species.
  • Contains a lone pair of electrons.
  • Nucleophilic and tetrahedral ($sp^3$) hybridization).
Free Radicals:

  • Neutral species with an unpaired electron.
  • Typically highly reactive.
  • Planar or pyramidal structure with  $sp^2$ or $sp^3$ hybridization.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Stability Order of Carbocations:
$\text{Tertiary > Secondary > Primary > Methyl}$
  • Explanation: Due to hyperconjugation and inductive effects.
  • Stability Order of Carbanions:
$\text{Methyl > Primary > Secondary > Tertiary}$
  • Explanation: Due to electron repulsion in bulky groups.
  • Free Radical Stability:
$\text{Tertiary > Secondary > Primary > Methyl}$
  • Explanation: Due to hyperconjugation and resonance stabilization.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: Which carbanion is most stable: methyl, primary, secondary, or tertiary?
blocks.prompt: Which carbanion is most stable: methyl, primary, secondary, or tertiary?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing carbocation and carbanion stability trends.
  • Remember: Positive charges prefer more alkyl groups for stabilization, whereas negative charges prefer fewer.
  • Assuming free radicals are always the least stable.
  • Note: They can be stabilized by resonance and hyperconjugation.

modules.name: Electronic Effects: Inductive, Mesomeric, Hyperconjugation, and Electromeric

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Inductive (I-Effect):

  • Electron movement through sigma bonds.
  • The effect diminishes with distance from the substituent.
Mesomeric (M-Effect):

  • Electron movement through pi bonds and lone pairs.
  • Involves pi bonds and lone pairs.
  • Delocalization through resonance structures.
Hyperconjugation:

  • Sigma to pi delocalization/sigma to vacant p orbital / sigma to partially filled p-orbital
  • Stabilization energy through adjacent empty or partially filled p-orbitals.
Electromeric (E-Effect):

  • Temporary electron shift.
  • Involves multiple bonds.
  • Specific to reaction conditions and disappears once the reagent is removed.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Inductive Effect: Permanent, no specific formula, relative & diminishes with distance.
  • Mesomeric Effect: Permanent, represented by resonance structures.
  • Hyperconjugation: Permanent, related to stabilization energy through resonating structures.
  • Electromeric Effect: Temporary, reaction-specific, no permanent formula.

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text: Overgeneralizing Effects: For example, while a nitro group is generally electron-withdrawing, its impact can vary depending on its position relative to other substituents.

blocks.title: Additional Guidelines
blocks.text:
• Remember the acronym I M H E for the types of effects: Inductive, Mesomeric, Hyperconjugation, and Electromeric.
  • Priority order: Mesomeric /Resonance > Hyperconjugation > Inductive.
  • Distinguish the direction of electron movement: Inductive through sigma, Mesomeric through pi, Hyperconjugation through sigma-pi, Electromeric is temporary.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Acidic Strength: The ability to donate a proton ($H^+$); stronger acids dissociate more completely.

To check acidic strength, check stability of conjugate base.

• Basic Strength: The ability to accept a proton; stronger bases have a higher affinity for $H^+$.

To check basic strength, check the lone pair donation tendency.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• pH and pOH:
$pH = -\log[H^+]$

$pOH = -\log[OH^-]$

$pH + pOH = 14$ (at $25^\circ C$ for pure water).

  • Dissociation Constant:
For Acids: $K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}$; larger $K_a$ indicates a stronger acid.

For Bases: $K_b = \frac{[B^+][OH^-]}{[BOH]}$; larger $K_b$ indicates a stronger base.

  • Relation of $pK_a$ and  $pK_b$ :
$pK_a = -\log K_a$; lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid.

$pK_b = -\log K_b$; lower $pK_b$ means a stronger base.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text: Misinterpreting pKa Values: Students often overlook that a lower pKa value indicates a stronger acid. It's common to think that a higher number means stronger acidity, leading to incorrect conclusions about a compound's reactivity.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
Arrange the following in the correct order of basic strength:

$(A) \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2  $

$(B) \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{NH} $

$(C) \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{N}$
blocks.answer:
(A)$ \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2$ $\rightarrow$$(sp { }^3 )$ nitrogen

(B) $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{NH}$ $\rightarrow$ $( \mathrm{sp}^2)$ nitrogen

(C) $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{N}$ $\rightarrow$$ (sp )$ nitrogen

Basic strength  $\propto \frac{1}{\text { electronegativity }}$

So Basic strength order :- A>B>C

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Aromaticity is a property of cyclic, planar molecules with delocalized π-electrons that follow Hückel's rule (4n + 2 π-electrons), giving them extra stability.

Note: Non-aromatic - cyclic compounds which are neither aromatic nor anti-aromatic.

blocks.prompt: Which of the following compound will have more rotational energy barrier.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing aromaticity with simple conjugation; not all conjugated systems are aromatic.
  • Overlooking planarity: aromaticity requires the molecule to be completely planar.

blocks.title: Tautomerism or Desmo Tropism
blocks.text:
• Tautomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas due to the migration of active hydrogen between two atoms of a molecule.

• Desmo tropism means bond turning. [Desmos = Bond; Tropos = Turn]

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Tautomers exist in dynamic equilibrium.
    • By shifting of H–atom, bond also changes its position.

Condition for Tautomerism:

For carbonyl compounds: - Carbonyl compounds having at least one active-H (–H) show Tautomerism

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
Generally, %keto > %Enol

But sometimes, %keto < %Enol

For Example, 1. Aromatic Enol 2. Active methylene (1,3 dicarbonyl) compound 3. Cyclic 1,2 diketo compound
